The child does not call shop fertiliser a compost material. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any waste can go on the compost heap (polythene, tins, glass).

example.question: Which of these should NOT go on a compost heap?
example.correct_answer: Banana peelings

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks a compost heap is a general rubbish heap.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A polythene bag" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Dig up an old heap with a teacher. Ask what rotted and what did not.
misconceptions.feedback: Polythene, tins and glass do not rot and spoil the manure. Only things that were once plants, and animal dung, go on the heap.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks cooked food, meat and bones are good for compost.

example.question: Why are meat bones and cooked food kept out of the compost heap?
example.wrong_answer: They are the best food for a compost heap
example.correct_answer: They draw rats and flies and smell

misconceptions.cause: The child knows meat rots and so thinks it belongs.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They are the best food for a compost heap" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what comes to a heap with meat scraps in it, and whether the school garden needs those visitors.
misconceptions.feedback: Meat, bones and oily leftovers draw rats and flies. Peelings, leaves, grass and dung are better.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls shop fertiliser a compost material.

example.question: Which of these is made by rotting plant remains and dung?
example.correct_answer: Compost manure

misconceptions.cause: The child links manure, fertiliser and compost as one thing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Fertiliser bought from the shop" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a bag of fertiliser and a handful of compost. Ask where each one comes from.
misconceptions.feedback: Compost is made at home by rotting plant remains and dung. Fertiliser from the shop is made in a factory. They are not the same.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Heaps one kind of material only (all dry sticks or all wet peelings).

example.question: What makes the best compost heap?
example.wrong_answer: Dry and fresh materials mixed in layers
example.correct_answer: Only wet peelings pressed into one heap

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks more of one good thing is better.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Dry and fresh materials mixed in layers" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make two small heaps, one with one material and one with a mix. Compare them after a month.
misconceptions.feedback: A mix of dry and fresh material in layers rots best. Dry material lets in air and fresh material gives moisture and food for the rotting.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the heap dry and open, or soaks it with water.

example.question: What does a compost heap need while it rots?
example.wrong_answer: To be kept dry and open to the sun
example.correct_answer: To be kept damp and covered

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks rotting happens by itself.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "To be kept dry and open to the sun" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a damp covered heap and a dry open heap after a month. Then flood one and smell it.
misconceptions.feedback: A heap rots best when it is damp, not soaking, and covered. Too dry and it stops rotting. Too wet and it goes smelly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Uses the compost before it has rotted.

example.question: When is compost ready to put on the garden?
example.wrong_answer: After one day, when the heap is made
example.correct_answer: When it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks compost is ready as soon as it is made.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "After one day, when the heap is made" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Open a young heap and an old heap side by side. Ask which still looks like peelings.
misconceptions.feedback: Waste needs weeks to rot. Compost is ready when it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Describe drip irrigation and why it saves water
skills.mastery: The child says drip irrigation gives water slowly, drop by drop, to the soil at the roots of the plant (through a tube or a bottle with a tiny hole), so little is lost to evaporation, run-off or watering the bare ground, and it uses less water than a hosepipe or pouring from a bucket. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

say why it saves water
say where the water goes

skills.name: Say how a simple drip system is set up and kept working
skills.mastery: The child puts the water container higher than the bed, makes a tiny hole in a bottle or tube, puts the dripping end beside the plant roots, fills the container, and checks that the hole is not blocked by soil. A big hole would let all the water out at once. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: put the set-up steps in order

misconceptions.error: Thinks drip irrigation pours water out quickly like a hosepipe.

example.question: How does drip irrigation give water to a plant?
example.wrong_answer: It pours a lot of water out very fast
example.correct_answer: It gives water slowly, drop by drop

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of a tap or hosepipe, not of a drip.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It pours a lot of water out very fast" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pierce a bottle with a pin hole and watch it. Ask how fast the water comes out.
misconceptions.feedback: Drip irrigation gives water slowly, drop by drop, so the soil can soak it up.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the drip falls on the leaves of the plant.

example.question: Where does the water from a drip system go?
example.wrong_answer: Onto the leaves of the plant
example.correct_answer: Into the soil at the roots

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of rain falling on the plant.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Onto the leaves of the plant" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask which part of the plant takes up water. Look at where a real drip tube ends.
misconceptions.feedback: The roots take up water, so the drip goes into the soil beside the roots.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks drip irrigation uses more water than a watering can.

example.question: Why does drip irrigation save water?
example.wrong_answer: It uses more water so the plant grows faster
example.correct_answer: Little water is lost and it goes to the roots

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks slow means more.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It uses more water so the plant grows faster" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Water one bed with a bucket and one by drip. Measure the water used.
misconceptions.feedback: Drip irrigation puts a small amount of water only where it is needed, so little is wasted.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the water container lower than the plants.

example.question: Where should the water container of a simple drip system be put?
example.wrong_answer: Lower than the bed, on the ground
example.correct_answer: Higher than the bed, on a stand

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think about water running downhill.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Lower than the bed, on the ground" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Raise and lower a bottle with a hole above a bed. Watch when the water flows.
misconceptions.feedback: Water runs downhill. The container must stand higher than the bed so the water drips out.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Makes a big hole so the water comes out faster.

example.question: How big should the hole in a drip bottle be?
example.wrong_answer: Big, so all the water comes out at once
example.correct_answer: Tiny, so the water comes out drop by drop

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks speed helps the plant.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Big, so all the water comes out at once" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make one tiny hole and one large hole in two bottles. Watch which waters a whole week.
misconceptions.feedback: A big hole empties the bottle at once and floods the plant. A tiny hole keeps the drip going for hours.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the drip far from the plant roots.

example.question: Where should the end of the drip tube be placed?
example.wrong_answer: Far from the plant, in the middle of the path
example.correct_answer: Next to the plant roots

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link the drip to where the roots take water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Far from the plant, in the middle of the path" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Dig up a small plant and show how close its roots are to the stem.
misconceptions.feedback: The water must fall where the roots are, so the drip end is placed next to the plant.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

skills.name: Say how to save fuel when cooking
skills.mastery: The child puts a lid on the pot, cuts food small, soaks hard foods such as beans before cooking, uses dry firewood, keeps the fire small once the pot boils, cooks several foods on one fire and uses an energy-saving jiko, and does not think a big flame cooks food faster. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the fuel-saving habit
say why a habit saves fuel

misconceptions.error: Thinks petrol or diesel is used as a cooking fuel at home.

example.question: Which of these is a fuel used for cooking at home?
example.correct_answer: Cooking gas

misconceptions.cause: The child knows petrol is a fuel and does not know it is for engines.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Petrol" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what burns in a jiko, a gas cooker and a car. Talk about why petrol is dangerous indoors.
misconceptions.feedback: Petrol and diesel are fuels for engines. They are not used to cook at home because they catch fire too easily.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks firewood is the only fuel at home.

example.question: Which list names only fuels used at home?
example.correct_answer: Firewood only, every home uses the same

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the fuel used in their own home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Firewood, charcoal, paraffin and gas" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask each learner which fuels their home uses and make one class list.
misconceptions.feedback: Homes use many fuels: firewood, charcoal, paraffin, cooking gas, biogas, electricity and solar.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up solid, liquid and gas fuels.

example.question: Which of these is a liquid fuel?
example.correct_answer: Paraffin

misconceptions.cause: The child links fuel names to the fire, not to the form of the fuel.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Charcoal" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour paraffin, hold charcoal and ask how each can be carried and stored.
misconceptions.feedback: Charcoal and firewood are solids, paraffin is a liquid, and cooking gas and biogas are gases.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Cooks with the lid off the pot.

example.question: Which habit saves fuel when boiling beans?
example.wrong_answer: Cooking with the lid off so you can watch
example.correct_answer: Cooking with a lid on the pot

misconceptions.cause: The child wants to watch the food and does not think the heat escapes.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cooking with the lid off so you can watch" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Boil two pots of water, one with a lid and one without, and time them.
misconceptions.feedback: A lid keeps the heat in so the food cooks faster and uses less fuel.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a big flame cooks food faster and so is better.

example.question: The pot is boiling. What should the cook do to save fuel?
example.wrong_answer: Add more wood so the flame is big
example.correct_answer: Make the fire small to keep it simmering

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks more fire means more cooking.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Add more wood so the flame is big" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask whether the water gets hotter than boiling when the flame is bigger.
misconceptions.feedback: Once water boils it does not get hotter. A big flame only wastes fuel.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks wet firewood is as good as dry firewood.

example.question: Which firewood saves the most fuel?
example.correct_answer: Dry wood

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks all wood burns the same.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wet, freshly cut wood" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Try to light a dry stick and a wet one and compare smoke and heat.
misconceptions.feedback: Wet wood makes smoke and gives little heat because the fire must first dry it. Dry wood burns well.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Name small wild animals that destroy crops and the damage they do
skills.mastery: The child links weaver birds and quelea birds to ripening grain, rats and mice to stored and planted grain, moles to roots and tubers, hares and rabbits to young vegetables, squirrels and monkeys to maize cobs and fruit, and knows bees and butterflies do not harm crops (they help it). skills.name: Say how a scarecrow is made and used
skills.mastery: The child makes the frame from two sticks in a cross, dresses it in old clothes, adds a hat, shiny or noisy things (old tins, strips of cloth or plastic that flap), sets it in the middle of the crop where it can be seen, moves it often, and does not use poison or traps because a scarecrow only scares animals away. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the material for a scarecrow
say why it must be moved

misconceptions.error: Thinks only big animals harm crops.

example.question: Which of these small animals can harm a maize field?
example.wrong_answer: None, only big animals harm crops
example.correct_answer: Birds, rats and squirrels

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of elephants and baboons in the news.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None, only big animals harm crops" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Walk the school plot and look for signs: pecked grain, tunnels, gnawed cobs.
misconceptions.feedback: Small animals such as birds, rats and squirrels also harm crops, because there are many of them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks bees and butterflies harm crops.

example.question: Which small animal does NOT harm the crop?
example.correct_answer: A bee on the bean flower

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks every small animal on a crop is a pest.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A rat in the maize" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Watch bees on a flowering crop. Ask what happens to the flower afterwards.
misconceptions.feedback: Bees and butterflies carry pollen between flowers and help crops to give seed and fruit.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Links an animal to the wrong damage (moles eating leaves, birds digging roots).

example.question: Which animal digs up roots and tubers under the ground?
example.correct_answer: A mole

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the animal is a pest but not what it eats.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A weaver bird" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Match pictures of the animals to pictures of the damage.
misconceptions.feedback: Birds peck grain, rats gnaw grain and cobs, and moles tunnel under the ground and eat roots and tubers.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a scarecrow can stay in one place all season.

example.question: Why is a scarecrow moved from place to place?
example.wrong_answer: It does not need to be moved at all
example.correct_answer: Animals get used to it if it never moves

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks it scares by being there.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It does not need to be moved at all" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a bird does after a week of seeing the same scarecrow that never moves.
misconceptions.feedback: Birds soon learn that a still scarecrow is harmless. Moving it and changing its clothes keeps them afraid.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a scarecrow, or poison and traps, should kill the animals.

example.question: What is a scarecrow made to do?
example.wrong_answer: Kill the animals that come near
example.correct_answer: Scare the animals away without hurting them

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks protecting crops means killing pests.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Kill the animals that come near" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask who also visits the plot, such as bees, and what poison would do to them.
misconceptions.feedback: A scarecrow only scares animals away. Poison and traps can harm many other animals as well.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Hides the scarecrow at the edge of the crop.

example.question: Where is the best place to stand a scarecrow?
example.wrong_answer: Hidden in the bush at the edge
example.correct_answer: In the middle of the crop, where it can be seen

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks it should be a surprise.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Hidden in the bush at the edge" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stand a scarecrow at the edge and in the middle and ask which one the bird can see from the sky.
misconceptions.feedback: Birds must see the scarecrow from far. Put it high in the middle of the crop.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks maize and beans have tiny seeds.

example.question: Which crop has a large seed, not a tiny one?
example.correct_answer: Maize

misconceptions.cause: The child links "seed" to any crop sown from seed.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Carrot" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Put a maize seed, a bean and a carrot seed in the hand and compare them.
misconceptions.feedback: Maize, beans and peas have large seeds. Carrot, spinach and coriander have tiny seeds.

misconceptions.error: Thinks cabbage and tomato are sown straight in the plot like carrot.

example.question: Which crop is usually started in a nursery and moved later?
example.correct_answer: Cabbage

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks all tiny seeds are treated the same.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Carrot" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask a farmer how he starts carrots and how he starts tomatoes.
misconceptions.feedback: Carrots do not like being moved, so they are sown where they will grow. Cabbage and tomato are started in a nursery.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks crops grown from cuttings, such as sweet potato vines, are sown from tiny seeds.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "By sowing tiny seeds" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a sweet potato vine cutting next to a packet of carrot seed.
misconceptions.feedback: Sweet potato is planted from vine cuttings, not seeds.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks lumps and stones in the seedbed do not matter.

example.question: How should the soil of a seedbed for tiny seeds be?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Rough, with lumps and stones" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sow tiny seeds in a lumpy bed and a fine bed and compare how many come up.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Sows tiny seeds deep.

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks deep soil protects the seeds.

misconceptions.help: Sow seeds at two depths and see which come up. A tiny seed has little food to push up.

misconceptions.error: Sows thickly and never thins the seedlings.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks tacking stitches are tiny and strong.

example.question: What are tacking stitches like?
example.correct_answer: Long and loose

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks all stitches are made to last.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Tiny and tight" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pull out a tacking stitch and then a back stitch and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Tacking stitches are long and loose so they are quick to make and easy to take out.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the tacking in the finished garment.

example.question: What is done with the tacking when the sewing is finished?
example.wrong_answer: It is left in the cloth
example.correct_answer: It is pulled out

misconceptions.cause: The child sees it as part of the stitching.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is left in the cloth" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a garment with tacking left in and ask what it looks like.
misconceptions.feedback: Tacking is only a guide. Pull it out when the final stitching is done.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Sews the final seam first and tacks after.

example.question: What comes first, tacking or the final stitching?
example.correct_answer: Tacking, then final stitching

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know tacking is a guide.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Final stitching, then tacking" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sew two slippery pieces without tacking and see them slide.
misconceptions.feedback: Tack first to hold the cloth, then sew the final stitching beside it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
